cur-fossil-florisbad.dateNote: In 1932 Thomas Dreyer found a partial skull at this spring in the Free State, South Africa. Electron-spin dating gives about 259,000 years (0.26 million years).
cur-fossil-florisbad.summary: A 259,000-year-old skull from a South African spring, close to the start of our own species.

q204323.placeNote: Born in South Africa and raised in Brooklyn, New York; the town is not recorded. The pin is just the middle of South Africa.

cur-fossil-sterkfontein.dateNote: In 1947 Robert Broom and John Robinson blasted out "Mrs Ples", the most complete skull of Australopithecus africanus, from these caves near Johannesburg. Its age is disputed: dates from flowstones in the cave put it at about 2.1–2.6 million years, but 2022 cosmogenic dating of the rock it lay in gives 3.4–3.6 million (Little Foot, from a deeper layer, about 3.7 million). The caves are part of the Cradle of Humankind World Heritage Site.

cur-fossil-makapansgat.dateNote: In 1947 James Kitching found the first Australopithecus bones in this limeworks cave in South Africa. The cave fill is about 3 million years old. It is part of the Cradle of Humankind World Heritage Site.

q19118036.dateNote: Uncertain place: SK 847 was found at Swartkrans, about 1 km from Sterkfontein. Wikidata and Wikipedia give Swartkrans the same point as Kromdraai, about 11 km away, so this pin may be several km out.

cur-fossil-rooidraai.dateNote: In 1976 James Kitching found a clutch of six eggs by the road at Rooidraai, in what is now Golden Gate Highlands National Park. In 2005 the embryos inside were shown to be Massospondylus, about 190 million years old (Early Jurassic). Pinned at the Wikidata point for the national park.
cur-fossil-rooidraai.summary: Where the oldest known dinosaur embryos, of Massospondylus, were found in South Africa.

cur-fossil-malapa.dateNote: On 15 August 2008 nine-year-old Matthew Berger, out with his father Lee Berger, spotted a fossil collarbone in this cave. The skeletons are about 1.98 million years old.
cur-fossil-malapa.summary: Two skeletons of a new human relative, Australopithecus sediba, were found in this South African cave in 2008.

cur-fossil-wonderwerk.dateNote: In 2012 Francesco Berna and Michael Chazan's team reported burnt bone and plant ash deep in this cave in the Northern Cape, South Africa. Early humans made the fires about 1 million years ago.
cur-fossil-wonderwerk.summary: A cave in South Africa with the oldest firm sign of fire made by early humans.

cur-fossil-rising-star.dateNote: In September 2013 two cavers squeezed through a gap 18 cm wide and found bones of a new human, Homo naledi. Over 1,500 pieces have come out. The bones are about 335,000–236,000 years old (about 0.3 million years).

cur-find-ga-mohana.dateNote: A rock shelter in the Kalahari, South Africa, where people about 105,000 years ago gathered 22 white calcite crystals and used ostrich eggshell, perhaps as water flasks (Wilkins et al., Nature, 2021).
